skill.hypothesis: Phenomenon: short-horizon reversal embedded within medium-horizon overextension and stress; Measurement object: persistent state combining signed return level, local path asymmetry, and stress magnitude rather than a pure one-day shock; Persistence hypothesis: in csi500-like small/mid-cap universes, recent losers with compressed continuation and elevated trading/range stress are more likely to mean-revert over subsequent horizons, while crowded winners tend to fade.
skill.grammar: Construct a reversal-state score by combining (i) signed medium-window return level, (ii) short-window delayed/recent return contrast as a recovery-vs-continuation proxy, and (iii) stress confirmation from range/volatility/extreme-return statistics; favor negative exposure to persistent positive trend states and positive exposure to recent downside extremes when accompanied by decelerating continuation.
skill.applicability: Most applicable in noisy, retail-dominated, mean-reverting cross-sections with limited long-trend persistence; weaker in strong benchmark-driven momentum regimes or during broad macro trend breaks.
successes: Use medium-horizon signed return level (ret20, rank_ret20, signedpow_ret20_half) as the core overextension measure, then confirm with short-horizon reversal-state terms (delay_ret5_1 positive, delta_ret5_1 negative).
Add path/stress modifiers through min/max/quantile of daily returns and range/volatility terms to distinguish exhausted selloffs from smooth trends.
Keep liquidity and volume terms secondary, using them only as confirmation of crowding/stress rather than the primary signal.
failures: Fails when momentum persistence dominates mean reversion, especially in strong policy/liquidity-driven rallies or crashes where overextension continues.
Fails when downside extremes reflect genuine information repricing rather than temporary dislocation, so positive loading on recent losers becomes a value trap.
Weakens in very low-dispersion regimes where range/volatility/extreme-return measurements carry little cross-sectional information.
